lead: The Lord has ascended, and the Church begins nine days of waiting for the Holy Spirit. Both readings lift our eyes upward. Paul, in chains, says he has not yet reached the goal and presses on toward “the heavenly call of God”, literally the call from above. In John, the one who comes from above is above all, speaks the words of God and gives the Spirit without measure. The Christian life is a race toward the One who has gone ahead of us, and he has promised to send us his Spirit for the running.

set: Paul writes to the Philippians from imprisonment (1:7, 13). Where he was held is debated: Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have all been proposed. Just before this reading he has warned against those who urged Gentile believers to be circumcised (3:2–3), and he has listed his own advantages: born of Israel, a Hebrew, a Pharisee, so zealous that he persecuted the church (3:5–6). All this he now counts as loss compared with knowing Christ (3:7–8).
Then comes a careful word. Knowing Christ is not a finished achievement. Some in Philippi may have thought they were already perfect; Paul, the great apostle, says that he himself has not arrived.
str: v. 12: not yet obtained, not yet at the goal; I press on, because Christ has made me his own.
vv. 13–14: one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind, straining forward, running for the prize.
v. 15: the mature think this way; where you think differently, God will make it clear.
kw: The same verb Paul used six verses earlier for himself as “a persecutor of the church” (3:6). Once he pursued Christians; now he pursues Christ. The energy is the same; the direction has been turned around.

Paul plays on the word: he strives to grasp, because he has already been grasped. “Christ Jesus has made me his own.” Our effort answers a hold that Christ laid on us first, on the road to Damascus and at our Baptism.

A runner leaning his whole body toward the line. St Gregory of Nyssa built on this word his teaching that the soul’s growth in God never ends: whoever finds God is drawn to seek him still more (in substance, Life of Moses).
vv: but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own.
Grace comes first, and it does not make us idle. Paul never says, “Christ has seized me, so I may rest.” He says, “so I run.”
forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead,

Paul does not forget the mercy shown to him; he speaks of it often. What he leaves behind is both his old pride and the weight of his old sin. The persecutor could have been crushed by his past. Forgiven, he looks forward.
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus.
The Greek speaks of the “upward call” (anō klēsis). In the week of the Ascension the picture is clear: the One who called us has gone up, and the prize is to be where he is.
ch: The Church teaches that the grace of final perseverance is a gift to be asked for, and that her children rightly hope for it (CCC 2016). Paul’s words guard against two errors: the despair that says the race is too long, and the pride that says the race is already won. The novena to the Holy Spirit, which many begin today, is the Church running this race on her knees, asking for the strength only the Spirit gives.

r.h: The one who comes from above is above all
set: These verses follow the last witness of John the Baptist in this Gospel: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and it is not clear whether vv. 31–36 continue the Baptist’s words or are the evangelist’s own reflection; many scholars think the latter. They gather up themes from the conversation with Nicodemus earlier in the chapter (3:11–13): heaven and earth, testimony, belief and life.
str: v. 31: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 32–33: his testimony refused, and accepted.
v. 34: the one sent speaks God’s words and gives the Spirit without measure.
vv. 35–36: the Father has given all to the Son; faith brings life, refusal remains under wrath.
kw: The same word Jesus used to Nicodemus: no one can see the kingdom without being born anōthen, “from above” or “anew” (3:3). The one who comes from above makes it possible for us to be born from above.
Literally “to set one’s seal”. Whoever accepts the Son’s testimony puts his own seal to the statement that God is true. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is our signature under God’s word.

The Greek does not say plainly who gives. It may mean that God gives the Spirit to the Son without measure, or that the Son gives the Spirit without measure. John’s Gospel teaches both: the Spirit rests on Jesus (1:32–33), and the risen Jesus breathes the Spirit on his disciples (20:22).
vv: The one who comes from above is above all;
Repeated at the end of the verse, this sentence frames the whole passage. The Ascension shows it in action: he who came down from heaven has gone back above all.
He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
The prophets received the Spirit for a task and a time. The Son has the fullness, and from that fullness he gives (1:16).
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life;

Not “will have” but “has”. Eternal life begins now, in faith, and is completed in glory. The word for God’s “wrath” (orgē) appears only here in this Gospel. It is not a temper but the sad result of turning away from the only source of life.
ch: St Augustine explains that the Spirit was given to the Son without measure, but to us by measure, each according to the gift he receives (in substance, Tractates on John 14). On the day of Pentecost Peter will say of the ascended Lord: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear” (Acts 2:33). This Gospel prepares us for that gift.

qa: Does “God’s wrath” mean that God loses his temper?

No. God has no passions as we do. Scripture speaks of his wrath to show that he is not indifferent to evil and that refusing him has real consequences. In John the contrast is between life and its absence: the Son offers life, and the one who refuses him stays where he was, outside it. God’s will is that all should be saved (1 Timothy 2:4).
rite: Today is the First Friday. Many Syro-Malabar families keep it with confession, the Holy Qurbana and devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. The Gospel fits the day: “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in his hands” (3:35). The heart that loves us is the heart of the Son into whose hands everything has been given.
study: What lies behind me that I need to leave behind, whether old pride or old guilt, so that I can run forward?
Where do I see the Spirit given to me “by measure” in my daily life, and what gift do I ask for in this novena?
